birddog.title: Bird Dog Protocol Simulation
birddog.scenarioIntro: It is 2:15 PM on a blistering Tuesday. You are operating a dozer on the South Bench. Suddenly, over the radio, you hear a frantic voice:
birddog.franticCall: "Jimmy's hurt bad! He's at the primary! Get help!"

problemPoints.distance: The "Primary" is 3 miles from the main gate
problemPoints.maze: Down a maze of unmapped haul roads
problemPoints.ambulance: The county ambulance driver has never been on your site
problemPoints.gps: Their GPS shows your pit as a blank grey void

birddog.youAreBirdDog: You are designated as the "Bird Dog"
birddog.birdDogExplanation: The term comes from aviation—a small, agile plane that guides heavy bombers to a target. In mining, you intercept the ambulance at the gate and physically lead them to the victim.
birddog.step1Question: The ambulance has been dispatched and is en route. What is your first action?
birddog.step1OptionA: Drive your pickup to the main gate immediately. Turn on flashers and strobes.
birddog.step1OptionB: Stay at the accident scene to help the victim directly
birddog.step1OptionC: Radio the ambulance with GPS coordinates
birddog.step1CorrectFeedback: Correct! Drive to the main gate immediately. Turn on flashers and strobes. You are the beacon.
birddog.step1IncorrectB: Incorrect. Staying at the scene wastes the 'Golden Hour'. Someone must guide the ambulance through the site.
birddog.step1IncorrectC: Incorrect. GPS doesn't work in the pit—you need to physically lead them.
birddog.step2Question: The ambulance arrives at the main gate. What do you do?
birddog.step2OptionA: Wave them through the gate and let them follow your dust
birddog.step2OptionB: Stop them completely. Pull up alongside window-to-window.
birddog.step2OptionC: Radio them instructions while driving ahead
birddog.step2CorrectFeedback: Correct! Stop them. Pull up alongside window-to-window for direct communication.
birddog.step2IncorrectA: Incorrect. Never just wave them through—they'll get lost.
birddog.step2IncorrectC: Incorrect. Radio communication isn't reliable—you need face-to-face contact.
birddog.step3Question: You're now window-to-window with the ambulance crew. What do you tell them?
birddog.step3OptionB: "Follow me. Stay in my tracks. The ramp is steep and slippery. Do not deviate."
birddog.step3OptionC: Provide a detailed map of the entire mine site
birddog.step3CorrectFeedback: Correct! Clear, specific instructions: Follow, stay in tracks, terrain warning, don't deviate.
birddog.step3IncorrectA: Incorrect. Too vague. They need specific instructions about following and terrain.
birddog.step3IncorrectC: Incorrect. This wastes critical time and they can't study while responding.
birddog.step4Question: You're now leading the ambulance through the mine. How do you drive?
birddog.step4OptionA: Drive as fast as possible—time is critical
birddog.step4OptionB: Stop at each intersection to make sure they're following
birddog.step4OptionC: Drive at a speed the ambulance can handle. You are their eyes.
birddog.step4CorrectFeedback: Correct! You are their eyes. Drive at a speed they can handle—you're tethered together.
birddog.step4IncorrectA: Incorrect. Going too fast means they can't keep up or might crash on unfamiliar terrain.
birddog.step4IncorrectB: Incorrect. Stops waste precious time from the 'Golden Hour'.
birddog.completeMessage: You successfully guided the ambulance to the victim.
birddog.takeaway1: The Bird Dog physically leads emergency vehicles through the site
birddog.takeaway3: Specific instructions: "Follow me, stay in my tracks, do not deviate"
birddog.takeaway4: Drive at a pace they can handle—you are their eyes
birddog.takeaway5: Without you, the "Golden Hour" runs out

radioDiscipline.title: Radio Discipline Training
radioDiscipline.panicIntro: In the Bird Dog scenario, the frantic call "Jimmy's hurt!" was dangerous. It was unstructured panic that doesn't convey critical information.
radioDiscipline.panicExample: "Jimmy's hurt bad! He's at the primary! Get help!"
radioDiscipline.seizeExplanation: To seize control of a radio channel during a crisis, use the universal interrupt phrase:
radioDiscipline.whyThreeExplanation: It's a cognitive "breaker." It cuts through the chatter of haul trucks and plant noise. When people hear it, they know to stop talking immediately.
radioDiscipline.completeScriptExample: "Break, Break, Break. Emergency at [Location]. [Nature of Incident]. Silence this frequency."
radioDiscipline.practiceInstruction: An emergency has occurred. Type the phrase you would use to seize control of the radio channel:
radioDiscipline.correctFeedback: Correct! "Break, Break, Break" seizes control of the radio channel during an emergency.
radioDiscipline.incorrectFeedback: Incorrect. The phrase is "Break, Break, Break" - said three times to cut through chatter.
radioDiscipline.hint: Hint: The phrase uses the word "Break" three times...
radioDiscipline.scenarioDescription: You witness a fire break out at the primary crusher. The radio is filled with normal haul truck chatter. Which is the correct emergency call?
radioDiscipline.scenarioOptionB: "Break, Break, Break. Emergency at the primary crusher. Structure fire in progress. Silence this frequency."
radioDiscipline.scenarioOptionC: "Dispatch, this is Unit 7, we have a situation..."
radioDiscipline.scenarioCorrect: ✓ Correct! This follows the proper protocol: Interrupt phrase + Location + Nature + Silence command.
radioDiscipline.scenarioIncorrect: ✗ Incorrect. The call should start with "Break, Break, Break" and include location, nature, and silence command.
radioDiscipline.completeMessage: You've learned to seize control of the radio during emergencies.

fireSuppression.title: Fire Suppression Simulation
fireSuppression.scenarioIntro: You are driving a 100-ton haul truck. You smell something sweet and pungent—hot hydraulic fluid. Suddenly, a warning light flashes: LOW HYDRAULIC PRESSURE.
fireSuppression.physicsExplanation1: A hydraulic hose has burst, spraying fluid at 3,000 PSI onto your turbocharger.
fireSuppression.physicsExplanation2: This isn't a liquid leak—it's an atomized mist.
fireSuppression.physicsExplanation3: When that mist hits the 1,000°F exhaust manifold, it doesn't just burn...
fireSuppression.physicsConclusion: It ignites with the ferocity of a blowtorch.
fireSuppression.fssExplanation: The fire suppression system (FSS) should trigger automatically, but sensors can be blocked by mud or grease. What do you do?
fireSuppression.scenarioOptionA: Wait for the fire suppression system to trigger automatically
fireSuppression.scenarioOptionB: Jump from the cab and run
fireSuppression.scenarioOptionC: Activate the fire suppression system manually
fireSuppression.scenarioWrongA: WRONG. Sensors can be blocked by mud or grease. You cannot wait for the machine to save you. You have seconds to act.
fireSuppression.scenarioWrongB: Partially correct instinct, but incomplete. You should evacuate, but first—you need to know about the ground level actuator.
fireSuppression.scenarioCorrectC: CORRECT. You have seconds. The fire suppression system (FSS) should trigger automatically, but sensors can fail. You cannot wait.
fireSuppression.actuatorExplanation: Every mining machine has a manual actuation button accessible from the ground (usually near the ladder or bumper).
fireSuppression.drillDescription: Imagine you are a bystander seeing this truck smoke. You run to the bumper. You see the red plunger.
fireSuppression.actionExplanation: This punctures a nitrogen cartridge, flooding the engine bay with dry chemical powder. You don't need to be in the cab to save the driver.
fireSuppression.criticalScenario: The fire is smoldering under the hood. You grab a hand-held extinguisher. Your instinct is to pop the hood to get a clear shot at the flames.
fireSuppression.flashoverExplanation: The fire inside the engine compartment has consumed most of the oxygen. It is "ventilation-limited." It is hot, hungry, and waiting.
fireSuppression.hoodOptionA: Pop the hood to get a clear shot at the flames
fireSuppression.hoodOptionB: Keep the hood closed and shoot through the grille or wheel wells
fireSuppression.hoodWrongA: DEADLY WRONG. Opening the hood introduces a massive rush of fresh oxygen. The superheated gases will EXPLODE outward in a backdraft. You will be engulfed in a fireball.
fireSuppression.hoodCorrectB: CORRECT! Keep the steel barrier between you and the beast. The fire inside is ventilation-limited—hot, hungry, and waiting for oxygen.
fireSuppression.hoodWrongC: WRONG. Every second counts. The fire will spread to the fuel tank, tires, and cab. You must act now with proper technique.
fireSuppression.extinguisherPoint1: Shoot the extinguisher chemical through the radiator grille
fireSuppression.extinguisherPoint3: Keep the steel barrier between you and the beast
fireSuppression.backdraftExplanation: If you open the hood, you introduce a massive rush of fresh oxygen. The result is a backdraft—superheated gases exploding outward. You will be engulfed in a fireball.
fireSuppression.survivalPoint1: Know the location of the ground level actuator on every machine
fireSuppression.survivalPoint2: Pull the pin, strike the button—you don't need to be in the cab
fireSuppression.survivalPoint3: NEVER open the hood—shoot through grille or wheel wells
fireSuppression.survivalPoint4: Backdraft kills—keep the steel barrier between you and the fire

loto.title: Interactive Simulation 1: The Virtual LOTO Procedure
loto.objective: You must correctly perform a complete LOTO procedure on a virtual conveyor belt drive motor to prepare for a coupling replacement.
loto.scenario: You are standing in front of Conveyor #3. A work order on your tablet instructs you to lock out the system for maintenance. You must navigate to the Motor Control Center (MCC) and identify the correct disconnect from a panel of similar switches.
loto.mccInstruction: You are at the MCC wall. Identify and select the correct disconnect for Conveyor #3.
loto.verifyOption: Return to conveyor and attempt to start it
loto.skipOption: Return to conveyor and begin work
loto.verificationTitle: You have returned to the conveyor control panel. Press the START button to verify the isolation.
loto.successMessage: The conveyor did not move. The system is safely locked out. You may proceed with maintenance.
loto.successLearning: Key Learning: The "Try" step confirmed you locked out the correct energy source. This verification is critical and must never be skipped.
loto.failureWrongMessage: The conveyor started because you locked out {{selected}} instead of Conveyor #3.
loto.failureWrongLearning: Key Learning: The "Try" step just saved your life. Without it, you would have begun work on energized equipment. Always verify before starting work.
loto.failureSkipMessage: You are preparing to work on the motor coupling. Suddenly, a simulated arc flash erupts from the junction box...
loto.failureSkipWhat: What happened? An unidentified secondary energy source was present. A coworker in another area reset a main breaker that back-fed the circuit.
loto.failureSkipLearning: Critical Lesson: The "Try" step would have revealed this hazard. NEVER skip verification. It's not locked out until you've tried it out!

highwall.title: Interactive Simulation 2: Highwall Hazard Identification
highwall.objective: Conduct a thorough workplace examination of a highwall following a heavy rainstorm and correctly identify all new or worsening ground control hazards.
highwall.scenario: You must perform the morning ground conditions exam. The environment is damp with puddles, indicating recent rainfall. You must inspect from multiple vantage points and identify hazards.
highwall.critical: Critical: Missing the tension crack at the crest will result in catastrophic failure.
highwall.findHazards: Click on each hazard area to identify and tag the hazard. You must find all {{count}} hazards.
highwall.whatTypeHazard: What type of hazard is this?
highwall.whatCorrectAction: What is the correct immediate action?
highwall.successMessage: You correctly identified all critical hazards. Final Score: {{score}}/100
highwall.successLearning: Key Learning: Thorough, systematic examinations from multiple vantage points are essential after weather events. The tension crack was the most critical indicator of imminent failure.
highwall.failureMessage: Later that day, the section of highwall with the tension crack fails catastrophically...
highwall.failureWhat: What went wrong? The tension crack at the crest was the most critical indicator of imminent failure.
highwall.failureLearning: Critical Lesson: More frequent and thorough examinations are required after rainfall. Tension cracks parallel to the highwall crest indicate that a large section is beginning to separate.
highwall.actionBarricade: Barricade and post the area immediately
highwall.actionMonitorScale: Monitor closely and report for scaling
highwall.actionScaleMaterial: Scale loose material from safe position

haulroad.title: Interactive Simulation 3: Navigating the Haul Road
haulroad.objective: Safely operate a large haul truck, recognize blind spot hazards, and correctly interpret spotter hand signals during backing maneuvers.
haulroad.scenarioPart1Desc: You're driving a 100-ton haul truck along the haul road. A smaller pickup truck will enter your blind spot.
haulroad.scenarioPart2Desc: At the dump point, you must back the truck to a berm using only the hand signals from a spotter visible in your mirrors.
haulroad.drivingScenario: You are driving forward. A pickup truck approaches from behind and begins to overtake on your right (passenger) side...
haulroad.pickupDisappeared: ⚠️ The pickup truck has disappeared from your right-side mirror!
haulroad.inBlindSpot: It's now in your largest blind spot
haulroad.radioRequest: 📻 Radio: "Driver, pull over to the right shoulder when you have a moment."
haulroad.blindSpotOptionA: Turn right toward the shoulder as instructed
haulroad.blindSpotOptionB: Hold position and radio back about the blind spot hazard
haulroad.blindSpotRadioResponse: 📻 You: "Negative, holding position. Vehicle in my right-side blind spot."
haulroad.blindSpotResolution: After 10 seconds, the pickup truck reappears in front of you.
haulroad.blindSpotClear: 📻 Radio: "Good hold, driver. That pickup is clear now."
haulroad.blindSpotLearning: Key Learning: Never maneuver without confirming your path is clear. You recognized the blind spot hazard and held position until it was safe.
haulroad.blindSpotFailureSubtitle: FAILED TO ACCOUNT FOR BLIND SPOT
haulroad.blindSpotFailureLearning: Critical Lesson: You turned into the pickup truck that was in your blind spot. Never maneuver without confirming your path is clear. The correct action was to hold position and radio back about the hazard.
haulroad.dumpPointInstruction: You've arrived at the stockpile. A spotter is positioned to guide you. They are visible in your driver's-side mirror.
haulroad.signalBackUpDesc: Both arms at sides, palms facing forward
haulroad.signalStopDesc: Arm extended, palm down, held rigidly
haulroad.respondLostVisual: 🔄 Turn so spotter is no longer visible
haulroad.spotterSuccessMessage: You successfully backed the haul truck to the berm using proper spotter communication.
haulroad.spotterSuccessLearning: Key Learning: You correctly interpreted all hand signals and maintained visual contact with your spotter throughout the maneuver.
haulroad.spotterSuccessLearning2: Clear communication and mutual understanding of signals is essential for safe equipment operation.
haulroad.visualLostLearning: Critical Lesson: The operator must stop the equipment immediately if they lose sight of the spotter for any reason. Never proceed without visual confirmation.
haulroad.wrongSignalMessage: Maneuver failed. You did not respond correctly to the spotter's "{{signal}}" signal.
haulroad.wrongSignalLearning: Key Learning: All personnel must use the exact same standardized hand signals. Misinterpretation can lead to deadly accidents.

crushSyndrome.title: Crush Syndrome Simulation
crushSyndrome.dp1Scenario: You are the first to arrive at a haul truck rollover. The operator is conscious but his leg is pinned under the truck bed. He is in severe pain and calling out for help.
crushSyndrome.dp1LearningObjective: Gather critical information to determine the correct medical protocol for crush injuries
crushSyndrome.dp1Warning: For crush injuries, TIME is the most critical factor in determining safe rescue protocol. The 15-minute threshold determines life or death.
crushSyndrome.dp1Question: What is your FIRST question to the trapped miner?
crushSyndrome.dp1OptionC: "Don't worry, we'll have you out in no time."
crushSyndrome.dp2CorrectMessage: You immediately identified the most critical information needed for a crush injury response.
crushSyndrome.dp2Scenario: The trapped miner tells you: "I've been stuck here for at least 20-25 minutes."
crushSyndrome.dp2Scenario2: A front-end loader arrives on scene, capable of lifting the truck off him immediately. He's in pain and desperately wants to be freed.
crushSyndrome.dp2WhatHappens: What happens if you release now:
crushSyndrome.dp2Consequence1: Muscle cells have been dying for 20+ minutes
crushSyndrome.dp2Consequence2: Toxic potassium and myoglobin trapped in the leg
crushSyndrome.dp2Consequence3: Sudden release = toxin surge into bloodstream
crushSyndrome.dp2Consequence4: Result: Immediate cardiac arrest or kidney failure
crushSyndrome.dp2LearningObjective: Apply the counter-intuitive time-based protocol that subordinates instinct to medical knowledge
crushSyndrome.dp2OptionA: Use the loader to lift the truck immediately. He's in pain and needs to be freed now.
crushSyndrome.dp2OptionB: DO NOT LIFT THE TRUCK. Keep the victim warm, offer reassurance, and wait for paramedics to administer IV fluids before release.
crushSyndrome.dp3CorrectMessage: You resisted the powerful instinct to immediately free the victim. This decision saved his life.
crushSyndrome.dp3Scenario: Paramedics arrive within 8 minutes. They start an IV line and administer fluids to counteract the toxins that have built up in the crushed tissue. After several minutes of preparation, they give you the all-clear to lift the truck.
crushSyndrome.dp3Recovery: The victim is transported to the hospital and makes a full recovery.
crushSyndrome.passDescription: You successfully applied the counter-intuitive 15-minute protocol for crush injuries. By subordinating your natural instinct to disciplined medical knowledge, you prevented a fatal case of Crush Syndrome.
crushSyndrome.passLessThan15Desc: Release victim immediately - toxins haven't built up yet
crushSyndrome.passGreaterThan15: If entrapment > 15 minutes OR duration unknown:
crushSyndrome.passGreaterThan15Desc: DO NOT RELEASE - wait for paramedics to administer IV fluids first
crushSyndrome.passWhyMattersDesc: When crushed muscle is compressed for prolonged periods, dead cells release potassium and myoglobin. Sudden release floods these toxins into the bloodstream, causing immediate cardiac arrest or kidney failure. IV fluids must be administered BEFORE release to counteract the toxin surge.
crushSyndrome.failDescription: You lifted the truck. The sudden release of pressure sent a surge of toxins from his crushed leg into his bloodstream. Within seconds, his heart stopped beating. Your attempt to help was fatal.
crushSyndrome.failPoint1: Entrapment duration was 20-25 minutes (>15 minute threshold)
crushSyndrome.failPoint2: Dead muscle cells had released toxic potassium and myoglobin
crushSyndrome.failPoint3: Sudden release flooded toxins into central circulation
crushSyndrome.failPoint4: Toxin surge caused immediate fatal cardiac arrhythmia
crushSyndrome.failPoint5: Natural instinct to "help immediately" overrode medical protocol
crushSyndrome.failMedicalFactDesc: "Crush Syndrome has a mortality rate of 40-50% if toxins are released without prior IV fluid administration. The first 15 minutes of entrapment are the critical decision point. After 15 minutes, DO NOT RELEASE until medical intervention."
crushSyndrome.failCorrectProtocolDesc: Keep victim warm and immobile. Reassure them. Explain why you cannot lift yet. Wait for paramedics to start IV fluids to counteract toxins BEFORE releasing the crushing force.

groundFailure.title: Ground Failure Simulation
groundFailure.dp1Scenario: You are operating a front-end loader at the base of a 55-foot highwall after a heavy rainstorm. You notice new tension cracks on the bench above and a small trickle of water seeping from the face that wasn't there before.
groundFailure.dp1LearningObjective: Recognize and correctly respond to warning signs of imminent ground failure
groundFailure.dp1OptionA: It's probably just settling from the rain. Continue loading—you have a quota to meet.
groundFailure.dp1OptionB: Stop work immediately, move the loader to a safe distance, and use the radio to report the hazardous conditions.
groundFailure.dp1OptionC: Quickly finish loading the current truck to meet your quota, then report it at the end of the shift.
groundFailure.dp2CorrectMessage: You reported the hazard and moved to a safe location. Excellent situational awareness.
groundFailure.dp2Scenario: Later, you are assigned to load from a stockpile that has a very steep face. Your supervisor tells you to dig into the base (toe) of the stockpile to get material out faster.
groundFailure.dp2LearningObjective: Identify and refuse to perform work involving unsafe stockpile procedures
groundFailure.dp2OptionA: Follow the supervisor's instructions and dig into the base (toe) of the stockpile.
groundFailure.dp2OptionB: Refuse the unsafe task and explain that digging into the toe over-steepens the pile and creates a collapse hazard.
groundFailure.dp3CorrectMessage: You refused the unsafe work assignment. Your supervisor reassigns the task with proper ground control measures.
groundFailure.dp3Scenario: You have successfully navigated both hazard scenarios. Now proceed to park your equipment safely.
groundFailure.passDescription: You successfully identified ground instability warning signs, reported them immediately, and refused unsafe work practices. Your adherence to safety protocols prevented a potential fatality.
groundFailure.passLearning1: Tension cracks and water seepage are critical warning signs of ground failure
groundFailure.passLearning2: Production quotas never justify working in unsafe conditions
groundFailure.passLearning3: Digging into the toe of stockpiles over-steepens the face and causes collapses
groundFailure.passLearning4: Every miner has the right and responsibility to refuse unsafe work
groundFailure.fail1Description: You ignored clear warning signs of an unstable highwall. The saturated ground gave way, and the 55-foot highwall collapsed, engulfing your loader. You did not survive.
groundFailure.fail1Point1: Tension cracks indicated imminent ground failure
groundFailure.fail1Point2: Water seepage after rain severely weakens slope stability
groundFailure.fail1Point3: Production pressure led to dangerous normalization of risk
groundFailure.fail1Point4: Delaying hazard reporting kept you in the danger zone
groundFailure.fail1InvestigationDesc: "The accident was caused by the miner's failure to recognize and respond to obvious signs of ground instability following adverse weather conditions."
groundFailure.fail2Description: As you dug into the base of the over-steepened stockpile, the pile collapsed. Tons of material buried the front of your loader and crushed the cab. You did not survive.
groundFailure.fail2Point1: Digging into the toe removes critical support material
groundFailure.fail2Point3: This was described as "normal mining method" - dangerous normalization
groundFailure.fail2Point4: You failed to exercise your right to refuse unsafe work
groundFailure.fail2BestPracticeDesc: "Material shall be drawn from stockpiles and surge piles in a manner that minimizes the hazard of material falling or sliding from the top."

thermalStress.title: Thermal Stress Emergency
thermalStress.description: Recognize and respond to heat exhaustion and heat stroke
thermalStress.recognitionScenario: It's a hot summer afternoon (95°F, 70% humidity). You're working near the crusher when your coworker, Mike, who has been shoveling material for the past hour, walks over looking pale. He's sweating heavily, his skin is clammy, and he says he feels weak and dizzy. He mentions he has a headache and feels nauseous.
thermalStress.initialScenario: Mike is now in the shaded break area. He's sitting down but still appears weak, dizzy, and is sweating profusely. His skin is pale and clammy. What is the correct immediate first aid?
thermalStress.monitoringScenario: After 10 minutes of cooling treatment, Mike is still weak and dizzy. He's no longer sweating as much, and his skin feels warmer and drier than before. He seems slightly confused and can't remember what day it is. What should you do?
thermalStress.preventionScenario: Mike recovers fully after hospital treatment. The safety manager asks you to help identify what led to this incident. Upon investigation, you learn: Mike is a new miner (2nd week), it was his first hot day on the job, he skipped breakfast, drank only one bottle of water during his shift, and was not given a heat acclimatization schedule. What was the PRIMARY preventable cause?

chemicalSpill.title: Chemical Spill Response

protocolSteps.rescue: RESCUE: Check for injuries, evacuate contaminated persons
protocolSteps.confine: CONFINE: Eliminate ignition sources, prevent spread
protocolSteps.report: REPORT: Notify supervisor and emergency responders
protocolSteps.secure: SECURE: Control access to prevent unauthorized entry
protocolSteps.cleanup: CLEANUP: Trained personnel only, with proper PPE

chemicalSpill.discoveryScenario: You are walking past the fueling station when you notice a strong diesel fuel odor. You see approximately 10 gallons of diesel fuel pooling on the ground near a parked haul truck. The fuel is flowing toward a storm drain 20 feet away. A front-end loader is idling nearby, and you can see sparks from a cutting torch being used in the maintenance shop about 50 feet away.
chemicalSpill.reportScenario: You have secured the ignition sources. The diesel is still flowing toward the storm drain. What is your next critical step?
chemicalSpill.secureScenario: The spill response team is en route (ETA 5 minutes). People are walking near the spill area, and vehicles are still moving through the fueling station. What should you do while waiting for the response team?
chemicalSpill.cleanupScenario: The spill response team arrives with PPE and equipment. The team leader asks if you want to assist with cleanup. You have safety glasses and work gloves, but no other PPE. What should you do?
chemicalSpill.followupScenario: The spill is now cleaned up. All contaminated materials are in proper hazardous waste drums. Your clothing has some diesel stains from the initial response. What should you do?
